overview: Celtiberians were communities of inland Iberia, with cities, distinct local identities and a Celtic language. This imported outline covers far too much of the peninsula, and its 1500 to 500 BCE interval precedes the best documented Celtiberian towns. The examples below are explicitly later Iron Age and Roman-period evidence, not a picture of a single Bronze Age kingdom.

periods.title: Later Iron Age communities
periods.summary: Urban life and regional traditions developed before Rome defeated Numantia.

periods.title: Communities under Roman rule
periods.summary: Local objects and written Celtiberian continued while institutions and writing practices changed.

items.text: The archaeological reconstruction at Numantia presents a rectangular house with three rooms. The front room combines grain grinding and weaving, with a hatch down to a cellar. This is a model of later Celtiberian domestic space, not an intact ancient house with its original furniture.

In the same reconstruction, the central hearth room was used for eating, sleeping and family gatherings. Storage occupied the back, and a side door led to an animal pen. Household space had to accommodate people, provisions, tools and livestock, sometimes very close together.

A 2024 study examined four storage contexts from the Celtiberian town destroyed in 133 BCE: an attached storeroom, part of an underground cellar and two cupboards. These protected spaces preserve pottery used for storing, cooking and serving. Archaeologists can distinguish kitchen tasks without finding a written shopping list.

The storage deposits also contained evidence of textile work and brooch manufacture. A room used to keep supplies could hold craft equipment too. These finds connect ordinary domestic storage with the production of clothing and the metal fasteners that kept it together.

Researchers sampled six grinding tools and fourteen pottery vessels from Numantia, spanning the Late Iron Age and Roman occupations. Starch traces revealed cereals, oats, acorns and legumes. The tiny residues preserve food evidence that a spectacular weapon or jewel cannot provide.

The plant study found evidence for both cultivation and seasonal gathering. Acorns linked households to nearby oak woodland; altered starch also indicated heating during preparation. The results show continuity across political changes, although they do not give us an exact ancient recipe or a complete menu.

Numantia’s especially distinctive painted pottery series belongs to the first century BCE, after the famous siege. Potters painted black designs on red clay using iron oxide, and also made multicolored vessels. Their birds, fish and human figures show that artistic traditions continued after military defeat.

sections.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word

items.text: A bronze hospitality token from La Caridad at Caminreal dates to the late second or early first century BCE. Such objects recorded agreements with reciprocal obligations between people, family groups or communities. A portable piece of metal could preserve a relationship extending beyond its owner’s household.

The Museo de Zaragoza preserves a silver coin from Turiasu, modern Tarazona, dated 100 to 50 BCE. Local minting gave a city a recognizable presence in everyday exchange. This is later evidence for urban institutions, not proof that the map’s vast earlier territory shared one currency.

A first-century BCE bronze text from Contrebia Belaisca records a dispute about land sold for an irrigation channel. Salduie wanted the canal; Alaun objected, and the judges ruled for Salduie. Getting water to crops required negotiation and legal decisions as well as digging.

Writing sample: the Novallas bronze has “LITANOM” in line 3, interpreted by its editors as a form meaning “wide.” The Celtiberian text uses Latin capital letters and dates around the late Roman Republic or early Augustus. This short, qualified translation is possible even though the complete fragment remains incompletely understood.

Scipio’s army surrounded Numantia with camps and barriers in 134 to 133 BCE, aiming to force surrender through hunger. The town fell in 133 BCE, and survivors were taken captive. This was a devastating local conquest; it must not be described as the instant disappearance of every Celtiberian community.

ending.text: Roman conquest and administration gradually transformed Celtiberian communities. Numantia’s fall in 133 BCE was a major event, but later pottery and written Celtiberian demonstrate continuing local life. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is much too early to mark the end of these communities.
